CuBr for KA 2  Reaction: En Route to Propargylic Amines Bearing a 
Quaternary Carbon Center † 
Xinjun Tang, a Jinqiang Kuang,a Xue Zhang,a and Shengming Ma*a, b 
Received (in XXX, XXX) Xth XXXXXXXXX 20XX, Accepted Xth XXXXXXXXX 20XX 
DOI: 10.1039/b000000x 5 
A highly efficient CuBr-catalyzed coupling of ketones, amines 
and alkynes (KA 2 ) forming propargylic amines bearing a 
quaternary carbon center with so far the broadest scope has 
been developed. 
Propargylic amines are important and useful buildin g blocks in 
10 
the synthesis of natural products and bioactive com pounds.1 The 
most straight forward well9established approach is the direct 
couplings of aldehyde9amine9alkyne (A 3) forming secondary 
propargylic amines.2,3  However, the three9component couplings 
of ketone 9amine9alkyne (KA 2) have been largely underdeveloped 15 
due to the extremely lower reactivity of ketones ob served in this 
reaction.4 The most commonly used catalysts are copper based: 599 
For example, Larsen et al. reported only one exampl e that 
relatively expensive and inconvenient Cu(OTf)2 (10 mol%) could 
catalyze the reaction of 19octyne, cyclohexanone an d benzyl920 
amine to afford the corresponding propargylic amine  in 80% 
yield;5 CuCl2 has also been used as the catalyst, however, the 
ketones must be activated by the addition of 50 mol% of Ti(OEt)4 
with a very slow reaction rate; 6 Ramón et al. utilized Cu(OH) x9
Fe 3O4 for such a transformation  of phenylacetylene with  3925 
pentanone or acetophenone and hexahydro9pyridine  yielding the 
propargylic amines in very low yields (29938% yield s) taking 7 
days.7 As a comparsion, Cu(I) seems much less active: Van  der 
Eychen et al. applied CuI (20 mol%) to yield the pr oparglic 
amine in 30% yield from the single reaction of phen ylacetylene, 30 
acetone and PMB9NH 2, which should be conducted under the 
mediation of microwave. 8 Thus, the challenge remains in the 
extremely narrow scope of the ketones, slow reactio n rate, and 
large amounts of reagents applied. Remarkably, scre ening of 
cheap Cu(I) catalysts and solvents in this laboratory revealed that 35 
this reaction is indeed particularly rapid and effi cient just with 
CuBr as the catalyst in toluene. Herein, we wish to report a highly 
efficient CuBr9catalyzed coupling of ketones, amines and alkynes 
forming propargylic amines bearing a quaternary car bon center 
with a most broad scope. 40 
 
Our initial work began with phenylacetylene 1a , a rather 
challenging acyclic 29hexanone 2a 4 and pyrrolidine  3a  under the 
catalysis of Cu(I). For the purpose of removing the in9situ formed 
water in the step of ketiminium formation, 4 Å mole cular sieves 45 
(MS) were added. After numerous trials, we were hap py to find 
that the reaction of 1a  (1 equiv), 2a  (1.1 equiv), 3a  (1.1 equiv) 
and CuI (10 mol%) in the presence of 4 Å MS (300 mg •mL 91) in 
toluene with stirring at 100 oC for 3 h afforded the propargylic 
amine 4a  in 88% yield (Table 1, entry 1)! Other solvents ga ve 50 
lower yields (Table 1, entries 294). When we used C uCl as 
catalyst, the yield was improved to 98% (Table 1, e ntry 5)! To 
our delight, a quantative yield was obtained when C uBr was 
applied (Table 1, entry 6). Further screening led t o the 
observation that this catalytic protocol is highly efficient: 1.5 55 
mol% of CuBr is enough to produce 4a  in a quantative yield 
within 1 h (Table 1, entry 9)! Further reducing the  reaction time 
led to a lower yield (Table 1, entry 10). When we c hanged the 
ratio of the starting material, the yield dropped ( Table 1, entry 
11). Thus, 1a  (1 equiv), 2a  (1.1 equiv), 3a  (1.1 equiv), CuBr (1.5 60 
mol%) and 4 Å MS (300 mg •mL 91) in toluene at 100 oC were 
defined as the optimized reaction conditions for further study.

afforded excellent yields of the products (Table 2,  entries 195). 
The reaction could also be extended to terminal alk yl9substituted 
alkynes such as 19octyne 1f , which gave the product in 85% yield 
(Table 2, entry 6). Moreover, terminal propargylic alcohol 1g  and 5 
protected propargylic alcohol 1h  are also suitable for this reaction 
yielding products 4g  and 4h in 86% and 78% yields, respectively, 
showing the functionality9tolerance ability of this protocol (Table 
2, entries 7 and 8). The hydroxyl group and TBS pro tected 
hydroxyl group of the propargylic amines 4g  and 4h  could be 10 
easily converted into other functional groups, whic h demonstrate 
the potential of this method.

Encouraged by these results we further investigated  a range of 
different ketones with phenylacetylene 1a  as the standard alkyne. 
The reaction showed a very broad substrate scope: n ot 
surprisingly, methyl ketones, such as 29butanone 2b , 29octanone 
2c , benzylacetone  2d  and 39methyl929butanone 2e  all afforded 25 
propargylic amines 4i 94l in 80~89% yields (Table 3, entries 194); 
the reaction of ethyl ketone also worked (Table 3, entry 5); even 
with heptane949one 2g , the yield of propargylic amine 4n  is 66% 
although 5% of CuBr was applied (Table 3, entry 6);  when 
cyclohexanone 2h  was used, the corresponding product 4o  was 30 
yielded in 93% (Table 3, entry 7).

The reaction may also be extended to other cyclic a mines such 
40 
as morphine and piperidine with relatively lower yi elds (Scheme 
1). Other acyclic amines, such as benzylamine and dibenzylamine, 
do not work under the current reaction condition, i ndicating the 
effect of amine on this protocol. 
 45 
Scheme 1 Cyclic Amines in KA 2 Reaction . 
It is worthwhile to note that aromatic ketones, which are totally 
inactive in the recently reported methods, 6 also work in this 
protocol: with 10 mol% of CuBr the corresponding pr oduct 4r  
was formed in 46% yield (Eq. 1). 7 50 
  
It is easy to conduct the reaction on 50 mmol scale  in benzene 
to afford 4a  and 4g  in 92% and 95% yields just using a Dean9
Stark trap to remove the in9situ formed water in th e step of 
ketiminium formation (Scheme 2), thus, the addition  of the 55 
molecular sieves is not necessary in any large scal e practical 
application. 
Scheme 2 Approach to Propargylic Amine ( 4) on 50 mmol Scale 
Using a Dean9Stark Trap. 60 
Conclusions 
In summary, we have developed a highly efficient Cu Br9
catalyzed direct coupling of unactivated ketones, a mines and 
alkynes to form propargylic amines bearing a quater nary carbon 
center. The mild reaction conditions, the broad sco pe of the 65 
substrates and the high efficiency of the reaction show the 
potentially synthetic utility of this method. 10912 Further studies 
including the asymmetric studies and the applicatio n of the 
propargylic amines are being conducted in our laboratory.
